The Fast Endpoint and Speed Comparison

Source: vignettes/fast-endpoint.Rmd
fast-endpoint.Rmd

Introduction

TabPFN-3.5 ships in several variants. The Fast checkpoint (3.5-fast) is a distilled model that delivers up to ~6x faster inference than the base 3.5 model, while keeping the same fit/predict workflow and the same prediction types (numeric, quantiles, conf_int). Select it with model_version = "3.5-fast".

This vignette benchmarks the base 3.5 and the 3.5-fast endpoints on a small synthetic regression problem to give a feel for the speedup.

Requires tabpfn >= 9.0.0. Upgrade with setup_tabpfn(upgrade = TRUE).

Data

A synthetic non-linear regression problem — enough rows for the timing to be meaningful:

set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
p <- 8
X <- as.data.frame(matrix(runif(n * p), ncol = p))
names(X) <- paste0("x", seq_len(p))

y <- sin(3 * X$x1) + 2 * X$x2 - 1.5 * X$x3^2 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.1)

Benchmark

Time fit() + predict() for the base 3.5 model and the 3.5-fast model. A warm-up fit is included so the first call’s one-off overhead (CUDA kernel compilation, model load) doesn’t dominate the numbers:

benchmark_endpoint <- function(model_version) {
  # warm-up
  tab_pfn_regression(X, y, model_version = model_version, device = "auto")

  t <- system.time({
    m <- tab_pfn_regression(X, y, model_version = model_version, device = "auto")
    predict(m, X, type = "numeric")
  })
  t[["elapsed"]]
}

time_base <- benchmark_endpoint("3.5")
time_fast <- benchmark_endpoint("3.5-fast")

results <- data.frame(
  Endpoint = c("3.5 (base)", "3.5-fast"),
  Elapsed_s = round(c(time_base, time_fast), 3),
  Relative = round(c(time_base, time_fast) / time_fast, 2)
)

knitr::kable(results, caption = "fit + predict elapsed time (1000 x 8 regression)")
fit + predict elapsed time (1000 x 8 regression)
Endpoint Elapsed_s Relative
3.5 (base) 7.23 5.09
3.5-fast 1.42 1.00

The Relative column expresses each endpoint’s time relative to Fast (1.00), so the base model’s value is the observed speedup of using 3.5-fast.

Predictions still match

Fast isn’t just faster — it returns the same prediction types:

m_fast <- tab_pfn_regression(X, y, model_version = "3.5-fast", device = "auto")

predict(m_fast, X, type = "numeric")
## # A tibble: 1,000 × 1
##    .pred
##    <dbl>
##  1 0.602
##  2 0.874
##  3 0.634
##  4 1.98 
##  5 0.740
##  6 0.504
##  7 0.786
##  8 2.11 
##  9 2.19 
## 10 1.19 
## # ℹ 990 more rows
predict(m_fast, X, type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
## # A tibble: 1,000 × 3
##    .pred_q025 .pred_q050 .pred_q075
##         <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
##  1      0.528      0.595      0.671
##  2      0.806      0.881      0.949
##  3      0.562      0.633      0.705
##  4      1.90       1.98       2.05 
##  5      0.658      0.741      0.819
##  6      0.440      0.504      0.571
##  7      0.720      0.787      0.850
##  8      2.04       2.11       2.18 
##  9      2.12       2.20       2.27 
## 10      1.12       1.19       1.25 
## # ℹ 990 more rows

Notes

  • Timings scale with dataset size; the Fast advantage is most visible on larger tables and repeated fits.
  • For the cloud “Thinking” endpoint (higher accuracy, point predictions only on the hosted API), see tab_pfn_regression(..., thinking_mode = TRUE).
  • A GPU is recommended for datasets past ~1000 rows.
